To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a simple model for the star formation rate of galaxies that successfully predicts the two-point galaxy clustering, galaxy-galaxy lens-ing, and spatial distribution of satellites in groups and clusters.
the star formation history of a galaxy depends on the formation time and mass of its halo, and that the spatial distribution of satellite galaxies is determined by their formation times.

(1) galaxy SFR is a function of halo mass assembly history, and as a result, quenched galaxies reside in more massive halos than star forming galaxies; (2) the halo assembly history is a function of the galaxy stellar mass and SED color; (3) the halo mass assembly history is also a function of the environment; and (4) the halo mass is the primary driver of the galaxy SFR, with the environment being the second-order driver.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of galaxy clusters, the largest virialised structures in the universe.

the study of galaxies in the local universe, and in particular with the study of their star formation rate (or equivalently their stellar mass) as a function of the mass of the dark matter halo in which they live.
the development and application of the age matching hypothesis to predict the SFR of a galaxy from its halo mass assembly history, and to test this hypothesis against new observations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the age matching model is able to reproduce all of the observational results in this paper, as well as the color-mass relation at z=0, the galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy-lensing measurements at z=0.2, the galaxy clustering measurements at z=1, and the color-mass relations at z=0 and z=1.

the galaxy-halo age matching model provides a simple and accurate description of galaxy properties and the galaxy-halo connection, and as such it is a useful tool for predicting galaxy evolution in the future.
the galaxy formation and evolution process is not yet well understood, although the basic physical processes that drive the process are known.

we are able to predict a large variety of galaxy clustering and galaxy-galaxy weak lensing measurements using a very simple model.
the star formation rates (SFRs) of galaxies are determined by the assembly history of their dark matter halos.
the star formation history of a galaxy is a strong function of the mass of its dark matter halo.
